title: Deterministic volume gap
formal:
For every fixed locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), is the following implication true?
\[
\bigl[\exists\text{ correct deterministic VOLUME algorithm }A:\lim_{n\to\infty}V_A(n)/n=0\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists\text{ correct deterministic VOLUME algorithm }B\ \exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1:\ V_B(n)\le C(1+\log^* n)\bigr].
\]
The function \(V_A(n)\) is the largest number of distinct vertices visited to determine one requested output on an allowed input with at most \(n\) vertices. Algorithms know the exact size \(N\) of their input graph, and distinct vertex identifiers lie in \(\{1,\ldots,N^2\}\). The model and input class are defined below.
definitions:
The problem \(\Pi\) fixes an integer degree bound \(\Delta\ge2\), an integer verification radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets, and a finite collection of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods. A neighborhood records the graph, its root, vertex input and output labels, degrees and local port numbers. Vertices within graph distance at most \(r\) are shown, with their induced edges and incident degrees. The rule ignores identifiers and graph size and is unchanged under rooted isomorphism preserving labels and ports. An output labeling is legal exactly when each vertex sees a permitted neighborhood.

Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), with every input labeling and every port numbering, including disconnected graphs. A port numbering assigns, independently at each vertex of degree \(d\), its incident edges bijectively to \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\); port numbers at opposite ends need not agree. There is no global graph-structure promise. A problem with unsatisfiable instances simply has no correct algorithm and cannot witness the premise.

A computation requested at vertex \(v\) starts with that vertex visited and with its identifier, input label, degree and port names, the problem description and exact graph size \(N\). A probe chooses an already visited vertex \(w\) and one of its ports, discovers the neighbor \(u\) reached by that edge, and returns \(u\)'s identifier, input label, degree and local port names. It adds \(u\) to the visited set. Repeated probes are permitted. A program can explore only by following edges from visited vertices: it cannot jump to a vertex merely by guessing its identifier. The returned input does not supply the identities of all unvisited neighbors for free.

Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including the initial vertex, is charged. Intermediate computation and working memory have no time or space bound but must terminate on every input. Each algorithm is one finite deterministic program, uniform over all graph sizes. There is no advice, random tape, preprocessing of the graph, persistent shared state or communication between separately requested output computations. Their answers nevertheless must combine into a valid labeling on every allowed instance and every distinct identifier assignment.

For \(n\ge1\), \(V_A(n)\) maximizes this visit count over all such instances with \(1\le N\le n\), all identifiers and all requested vertices. The exact size known to the algorithm in that maximization is \(N\), not the outer bound \(n\). For a correct terminating algorithm this maximum is finite. The constants and the programs in the implication may depend on the fixed problem \(\Pi\), including its degree bound and verification radius, but not on \(n\).

Define \(\log^*n\) as the number of successive applications of \(\log_2\) needed to reach a value at most one; in particular \(\log^*1=0\). The limit in the premise means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(n_0\) has \(V_A(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The all-\(n\) bound in the conclusion is equivalent to an eventual big-O bound after enlarging its constant to handle finitely many small sizes. The claim concerns deterministic connected exploration, not randomized VOLUME algorithms or local computation algorithms allowed to probe distant vertices.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication or a fixed LCL counterexample. A counterexample must include a correct sublinear-volume algorithm and prove that every correct deterministic algorithm \(B\) fails the iterated-logarithmic bound: for every \(C>0\) and \(n_0\), some \(n\ge n_0\) has \(V_B(n)>C(1+\log^*n)\). Randomized intermediate complexities, bounds for one graph promise, or an unproved assertion that an optimal algorithm exists do not suffice.
why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

sentences: The VOLUME model counts how many graph vertices are inspected to determine one requested output.
Separate deterministic queries must agree on a globally legal labeling without sharing mutable state.
The question asks whether every fixed locally checkable problem with sublinear volume also has iterated-logarithmic volume.
The graph degree, verification radius and label alphabets are fixed, while graph size and identifiers vary.
Recent constructions fill randomized complexity ranges but leave this deterministic gap unresolved.

source_formulation.text: Question 7.1 asks whether deterministic LCL volume can lie strictly between the iterated-logarithmic and linear scales, and conjectures that it cannot. The card expresses the conjecture as an implication between existence of algorithms, retaining the saved connected-probe, exact-size and polynomial-identifier conventions.
